name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,462

clue.text: A Parisian caught breaking wind in congress?

indicators.note: something breaking into another thing ends up lodged inside it

blocks.note: first part of a coil, something wound

explanation.surface: A Frenchwoman lets slip some flatulence in the middle of a formal assembly.
explanation.walkthrough: To wind is to COIL; UN plus C break into it to make COUNCIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A council is a formal assembly of people gathered to deliberate, as a congress is.

clue.text: Bubbly chap game to get blotto around noon

indicators.note: someone blotto is helplessly drunk, so these letters stagger out of order
around means wrapped about another piece

explanation.surface: A man starts a drinking game on fizz and is plastered by midday.
explanation.definitionFit: Bubbly is the informal name for sparkling wine, especially the French classic from Reims.

clue.text: One steering ship should avoid leading Republican tit

indicators.note: avoiding something means leaving it out, so a letter is dropped
leading picks out the letter at the head of the following word

explanation.surface: A captain is told to steer clear of a foolish Republican politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Tit looks like an insult or a bird; it is slang for a teat.
explanation.definitionFit: Tit is a slang word for a teat, and an udder is the milk-producing gland of a cow.

clue.text: Bird and a bear going round in very high spirits

indicators.note: going round turns the word to face the other way

explanation.surface: A cockerel and a bear dance in circles, both thrilled.
explanation.definitionFit: Cock-a-hoop is an idiom for being jubilant, delighted, boastfully elated.

clue.text: Tenor getting into row about a right crappy place?

indicators.note: getting into something means ending up inside it
about means wrapped round another piece

blocks.note: LINE, a row, split around the next piece

explanation.surface: An opera singer joins an argument about a dreadful venue.
explanation.walkthrough: Row reads as a quarrel, but it is a LINE; T goes into A R, which goes into LINE.
explanation.definitionFit: A latrine is a basic toilet, as in a camp or barracks, literally where one goes to defecate.

clue.text: Nick loses head in the sack - that's messed up

indicators.note: losing its head means the word drops its opening letter
one thing sitting in another is held within it

blocks.note: 'the sack' is slang for bed; it is split around the other piece
a notch is a nick; it loses its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone called Nick fails to get excited in bed, which is a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' reads as a man's name, but it is a notch; NOTCH loses N and sits inside BED.
explanation.definitionFit: Botched work is bungled or ruined through clumsiness, the same sense as a job that was messed up.

clue.text: Weightlifter's companion and I might ring last orders

blocks.note: first meaning: the weighted bar used in the gym
second meaning, split in two: the bell rung in a bar at closing time

explanation.walkthrough: In British pubs a bell is rung to call last orders before closing; read as BAR BELL, that is the second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A barbell is the long bar with weights at each end that a weightlifter trains with.

clue.text: Unit of beer model-type upset over head of studio

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the pieces upside down so they read bottom to top
lying over something means covering it all round
the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A beer-advertising model is unhappy with the studio boss.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hides a car joke: Tesla is also a car maker, and T comes from the Model T Ford.
explanation.definitionFit: The tesla is the SI unit of magnetic flux density, named after Nikola Tesla.

clue.text: Bit of computer kit in the Paris-Dakar rally?

definitions.text: Bit of computer kit in the Paris-Dakar rally?

blocks.note: the plain sense: a component of a PC that stores data
the setter's sense: the desert race is a tough, punishing journey by car

explanation.walkthrough: The Paris-Dakar rally is a famously gruelling off-road race across the Sahara, so the phrase can be read as a difficult motoring trip.
explanation.definitionFit: The storage unit inside a computer has a name that also describes a gruelling journey behind the wheel.

clue.text: Charge written up (Queen's bottom pinched)

indicators.note: in a down clue, written upwards means read from bottom to top
the bottom of a word in a down clue is its last letter

blocks.note: a ward is someone in another's charge

explanation.surface: A cheeky report of someone pinching the monarch's backside and being charged for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinched' looks like part of the joke, but it is the definition, as in a pinched face.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinched and drawn both describe a face that looks tired, thin and strained.

clue.text: Edward the VIII? A British tyrant half the time!

indicators.note: time is abbreviated to a letter that appears twice in the word, and only half of those occurrences stay

blocks.note: a dictator is a tyrant; one of its two Ts goes

explanation.surface: A jibe that the king who gave up his throne behaved like a tyrant half the time.
explanation.walkthrough: T is time; DICTATOR has two of them, and keeping only half of the Ts gives DICATOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward VIII famously renounced the British throne in 1936, so he is an example of someone who abdicates; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Country stronghold you raid in anger at the front

indicators.note: only what stands at the front of each of the following words is taken

blocks.note: opening letters of the five words

explanation.surface: A military report of storming a fortress in a fury.
explanation.definitionFit: Syria is a nation in the Middle East, bordering Turkey, Iraq and Lebanon.

clue.text: Parents to tour Rome at first, then here?

indicators.note: touring something means going all around it, so one piece surrounds another
at first points to the opening letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: Mum and Dad plan an Italian holiday, starting in Rome and then moving on somewhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the place the parents visit after Rome on their tour, so 'here' points to a city in Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Parma is a city in northern Italy, a natural stop for travellers continuing on from the capital.

clue.text: Nice dame I put out is a really cool woman

indicators.note: letters put out are knocked out of their order and set down differently

explanation.surface: A pleasant lady who has been snubbed turns frosty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' suggests the nice dame is offended, which fits the frosty answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice maiden is a woman seen as aloof and emotionally cold, which is what 'really cool' means here.

clue.text: Posh firm near Kent after good tip from Lord Sugar

indicators.note: a tip is the end point of something, here the very start of the following word

blocks.note: Kent is a county in the south-east of England

explanation.surface: Business advice from Alan Sugar about a smart company in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Sugar is the businessman of TV's The Apprentice; the clue splits him so that Sugar is the definition. U is crossword shorthand for upper-class.
explanation.definitionFit: Glucose is a simple sugar, the main carbohydrate the body uses for energy.

clue.text: Plain rude to mess around with a northern don

indicators.note: messing letters about scrambles their order

explanation.surface: It is simply impolite to fool about with a university lecturer from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: A don is a university teacher, especially at Oxford or Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unadorned has no decoration, which is what plain means when describing a style.

clue.text: Drinking like a setter? Don't start panicking!

indicators.note: not starting means the word is missing its first letter

blocks.note: flapping means panicking, minus its opening F

explanation.surface: A nervous crossword setter is told to stay calm while having a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Setter here is the dog breed, not the crossword compiler; dogs drink with their tongues.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog drinks by scooping water up with its tongue, which is called lapping.

clue.text: Police head new plan to ask for change in America

indicators.note: to police something is to bring it into order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The chief of police comes up with a fresh scheme for collecting money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Police head' reads as a chief constable, but Police is a verb working the letters of the next three words.
explanation.definitionFit: In American English, to panhandle is to beg in the street, asking passers-by for spare coins.

clue.text: Doctor assessing condition of long-winded patient?

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are altered

explanation.surface: A physician examining a patient who will not stop talking.
explanation.walkthrough: Long-winded usually means wordy; here it is taken literally as flatulent.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-winded patient, taken literally, suffers from wind, an excess of intestinal gas.

clue.text: In Spain, the PM turned on old American model

indicators.note: turned round means the pieces run the other way

explanation.surface: A Spanish prime minister falls out with a former US ally over politics.
explanation.walkthrough: Here 'on' means placed after: the turned Spanish article and prime minister follow the first two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An example is a model or pattern to be copied, as in setting an example for others.

clue.text: Shaven-headed folk who might who guard The Doors?

indicators.note: with its head shaved, the word loses its top letter

blocks.note: people on guard duty; the clue's doubled 'who' is as printed

explanation.surface: Bald bouncers guarding a gig by the band The Doors.
explanation.walkthrough: The Doors sounds like the rock band; doors are ways in. The clue has a stray repeated 'who' as published.
explanation.definitionFit: An entry is a way into a building, so entries are doorways or entrances.

clue.text: Crazy couple of people getting jiggy with it?

definitions.text: couple of people getting jiggy with it?

blocks.clueFragment: couple of people getting jiggy with it?
blocks.note: second meaning, whimsical: those who bonk, British slang for having sex

explanation.surface: A wild couple dancing energetically.
explanation.walkthrough: To bonk is British slang for having sex, so the second reading treats the answer as a plural noun: people who bonk.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonkers is informal British for mad, and the punning second sense makes a noun of people who bonk.

clue.text: Suits initially criticised medal won by those with the best knees?

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the next word
something won by people is held by them, so it sits inside

blocks.note: bees, from 'the bee's knees'; split around the next pieces
the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: Suits are criticised as an award goes to the people with the finest legs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The bee's knees' is an idiom for the very best, so bees are those with the best knees.
explanation.definitionFit: If an outfit becomes you it flatters you, the same as saying it suits you.

clue.text: Rubbish old git cites is all about me?

indicators.note: rubbish treats these letters as junk to be thrown together any old way

explanation.surface: A grumpy old man who keeps quoting himself is dismissed as rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: An egotistic person is self-centred and thinks everything revolves around themselves.

clue.text: Ecstasy Hoskins had with Her Maj and a flapper

blocks.note: the setter, Hoskins, would say 'I had', shortened

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of taking a drug with the Queen and a 1920s party girl.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves as I or me; a flapper sounds like a 1920s party girl but is something with wings.
explanation.definitionFit: An eider is a large sea duck, and a duck is a bird that flaps its wings.

clue.text: One's certain to do away with royal children

indicators.note: doing away with something gets rid of it, so a letter goes

blocks.note: R for royal or rex, removed

explanation.surface: Someone vows to abolish the monarchy's children.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue is a legal and formal word for offspring or descendants, as in 'died without issue'.

clue.text: I love almost everything about that one's sauce

indicators.note: almost all of something means it falls short by its last letter
something placed about another wraps around it

blocks.note: ALL, cut short, opens around the next piece

explanation.surface: Someone declares their passion for a particular sauce over all others.
explanation.walkthrough: ALL loses its last letter to make AL, which goes round I O; I (one) follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Aioli is a garlic mayonnaise from Provence, served as a sauce or dip.

clue.text: Foreigner is no gent, having sat on one

explanation.surface: A rude stranger sits on someone, which is hardly gentlemanly.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, sitting on one puts the first pieces above I.
explanation.definitionFit: An Omani is a person from Oman, so to a Briton such a person is a foreign national.

clue.text: Eats and drinks after ditching wife for date

indicators.note: one item is dropped and another taken up in its place

blocks.note: to wine is to drink wine

explanation.surface: A man wines and dines a new date after leaving his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls 'wines and dines'; W for wife becomes D for date.
explanation.definitionFit: To dine is to have a meal, so someone who dines eats.

clue.text: I made time up without delay

indicators.note: something made up is invented, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of catching up on lost time and acting promptly.
explanation.definitionFit: Immediate describes something happening at once, instantly and with no pause.

clue.text: Half-cut Barnes punches left-wingers? Ruddy quality!

indicators.note: cut by half means one half of the name is lost
something punching into another ends up inside it

blocks.note: Reds are socialists; split around the next piece

explanation.surface: A drunk man named Barnes starts a fight with some socialists, leaving them bloodied.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-cut is British slang for tipsy, but here it halves Barnes; ruddy can also be a mild British curse.
explanation.definitionFit: Redness is the property of being red, and a ruddy complexion is reddish in colour.

clue.text: Variety of glasses that browser should try on

indicators.note: trying on clothes means putting them around yourself, so one piece is worn by the other

explanation.surface: A shopper browsing for eyewear is urged to try on a few pairs.
explanation.walkthrough: A browser sounds like a shopper but is the web software Internet Explorer.
explanation.definitionFit: A species is a kind or sort, as in a variety of something distinct from others.
